extracted.intended_audience: calculus instructors and mathematics-education researchers (undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and using model-eliciting tasks (and related realistic problems) to measure and develop students' deep, transferrable understanding of calculus in undergraduate courses. Also includes analysis of instructor proof-presentation and student proof-writing via Toulmin's model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (teacher/user view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether tasks are set in a physical, theoretical, or abstract situation; often massaged or formatted such that it fits into an existing description. The students’ role is to recognize the expected concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tasks are contrived to fit existing descriptions, students are asked to 'recognize' rather than to mathematize the raw situation. This is an anti-pattern for eliciting deep understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library (selection of description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a student has assessed the situation, he/she must intelligently select the appropriate description from those that already exist in the 'library.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should help students become proficient at recognizing what to 'check out' from the library; students are expected to be able to explain their check-out decision. Reliance solely on this reduces transferability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures and Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures are linked to the choice of description(s) and the student is expected to accurately execute the appropriate procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dimension emphasizes correct execution of methods tied to chosen descriptions; when over-emphasized without sense-making, it fosters procedural (instrumental) understanding rather than conceptual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictions (sense-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the procedure’s result, the student is to make a sensible prediction about the given situation (e.g., check units, expected effects of changing a variable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include checks for reasonableness (units, parameter variations). Skilled problem solvers relate numerical results back to the situation and judge plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (hypothesized view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide realistic situations to students that usually do not quite fit into an existing description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks so they do not map neatly to textbook templates; this forces students to compose descriptions and develop deeper understanding rather than pattern-match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description (student-composed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students look at a situation, in the raw, and use calculus concepts to compose a description, not necessarily one that matches something in the library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to create mathematical descriptions (models) of the situation rather than selecting pre-existing formulas; this fosters ownership and transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate to Situation (assumptions and uncertainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: After producing results/predictions, students should identify what assumptions were made and how those assumptions affect applicability (margin of error, degrees of uncertainty, differences from alternative assumptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks should require students to articulate limitations, possible errors, and conditions under which conclusions hold (dashed-arrow in hypothesized diagram). This distinguishes deep understanding from rote application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership, flexibility, durability, transferability of understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: When a student composes the calculus description, he/she 'owns' it; such ownership allows building, deepening, and applying understanding in novel/unfamiliar situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction/tasks so students create and justify their own models; evaluate whether students can modify and apply their solutions in new contexts (cook analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-Eliciting Activities (MEAs) core characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: MEAs require students to go beyond short answers to produce sharable, manipulatable, modifiable, and reusable conceptual tools (models) for constructing, describing, explaining, manipulating, predicting, or controlling mathematically significant systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MEAs to prompt mathematizing: quantifying, dimensionalizing, coordinatizing, categorizing, algebratizing, and systematizing relevant objects, relationships, actions, patterns, and regularities. MEAs differ from traditional word problems in requiring creation of models and explicit assumption-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematizing vs decoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between creating mathematical descriptions from raw situations (mathematizing) and making meaning of already symbolically described situations (decoding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer tasks that require mathematizing to better measure/apply understanding; decoding tasks primarily assess translation of given symbolic descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task features that elicit calculus understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks should be realistic, raw, and require students to use calculus concepts to describe situations and arrive at predictions that can be extended to other situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks need not explicitly require computation of derivatives or integrals; instead, they should require modeling reasoning (e.g., Toy Train, Theater). Evaluate student ability to connect concepts (rate, accumulation) to situation and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tasks as measurement and learning opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: These tasks can be used before instruction to encourage students to develop their own understandings or after instruction to measure and deepen understanding while applying taught material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement MEAs both diagnostically and formatively; use resulting measurements to adjust instruction to prepare students for client disciplines. Research shows MEAs can lead students to invent or extend powerful constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toy Train Problem design criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Realistic design task: maximize mountain height, minimize track length, ensure track grade ≤10%; central calculus concepts are rate of change (derivative) and accumulation (integral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide raw topographic data; require relabeling contours, designing feasible paths (grade constraint), drawing diagrams, and describing decision process. Constrain time (e.g., 60 minutes) and require explanation for designers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theater Problem design criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling task: use arrival rates, capacities, and service rates to recommend arrival times and attendant staffing to minimize wait while preserving a buffer; central calculus concepts include rate of change, accumulation (integral), and derivative-integral relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include varying arrival rates (non-constant), realistic capacity assumptions, and ask for written recommendations with explanations. Balance minimization goals with operational constraints (attendants, buffer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Toulmin model components for analyzing mathematical proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Toulmin's six elements: Data (D), Conclusion (C), Warrant (W), Backing (B), Modal Qualifier (Q), Rebuttal (R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the full Toulmin scheme to analyze both instructor proof-presentations and student proofs; identify presence/absence and types of warrants, backing, qualifiers, and rebuttals. Inglis et al. (2007) recommend the full model over reduced versions for mathematicians' proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor-modeled level of detail as evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional instructors typically model the mathematical behavior (including level of detail) they expect from students; students appropriate modeled behavior in their proof-writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating student proofs, consider whether the instructor explicitly presented warrants, backing, qualifiers, and rebuttals. Lack of instructor modeling of certain elements predicts their absence in student work; thus, analyze teaching to explain student performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Toulmin analysis to link teaching to student work
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: analyze an instructor's presentation of proofs with Toulmin's model, then analyze student proofs to determine whether the taught/modelled argumentation predicts student proof-writing behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical analytic rubric for lecture-based, proof-intensive courses; applicable to any proof-based mathematics course to explain and predict student writing patterns (e.g., whether students include warrants/backing/qualifiers/rebuttals).
